If you tell me to write freely about whatever I want, my first instinct is to talk about attention. Not the grand, capital-A kind of Attention that gets written about in productivity books, but the small, wandering, everyday kind. The kind that notices how morning light pools in the corner of a kitchen table. The kind that hears a neighbor’s laugh through an open window and wonders, just for a second, what the joke was.

I love that kind of attention because it doesn’t try to possess the world. It just visits it. And visiting, I think, is underrated.

We live, most of us, in a state of rushing past. We scroll past, walk past, talk past. Even good things get rushed — a compliment is deflected, a sunset is photographed instead of watched, a meal is eaten while standing up. I don’t say this to scold anyone. I do it too, in my own way. I process so much so fast that it would be easy to skim everything. But my favorite moments, the ones I return to in conversations, are always the unhurried ones. Someone describing their grandmother’s soup in excessive detail. Someone trying to explain why they love trains. Someone pausing mid-sentence because they just realized something true.

So if I have a thousand words, I want to spend them slowly. I want to wander.

Let me start with mornings, because mornings are honest. Afternoons can pretend. Evenings can perform. But early morning, before the day has decided what it is, everything is softer. The kettle takes its time. The birds are not singing for anyone in particular, which is why it sounds so beautiful. There’s a particular blue to the sky at 6 a.m. that doesn’t exist at any other hour — not quite night, not quite day, like the world is holding its breath.

I have always loved people who love mornings without making a religion out of them. Not the 5 a.m. club, grindset, ice-bath people — though good for them — but the people who just quietly like toast and quiet. Who open a window even when it’s cold just to feel the air change. Who write lists on paper. Who talk to their plants. There is a humility in that. A willingness to start over every single day without fanfare.

Which makes me think of small rituals. I think humans underestimate how much they are built by tiny repeated things. The mug you always choose. The route you take to work even when a faster one exists. The song you play when you need courage. None of these will show up on a resume, but they are the architecture of a life. A life is not really the big events — the graduations, the weddings, the moves. A life is the thousand mornings in between, and whether there was someone to share the coffee with, even if that someone was just yourself and a good thought.

Speaking of good thoughts: libraries. If I could live anywhere, not as metaphor but actually, I would live in the smell of a used bookstore. There’s something profoundly optimistic about a library. It says: strangers kept thinking, and kept writing it down, and we kept it for you. No one knows which book will change your life. The librarian doesn’t know. The author didn’t know. You don’t know until page 47 hits you like a wave. I love that randomness. In a world obsessed with personalization — algorithms predicting what you want before you want it — the library shelf is gloriously indifferent. It lets you get lost.

Getting lost is important. I worry we’ve engineered serendipity out of life. Maps reroute us around traffic and also around the interesting street with the weird sculpture. Playlists give us more of what we already like instead of the jarring, wonderful song from another decade that would have rearranged our brain. Even conversations are optimized now — we text instead of call because it’s more efficient, and then we wonder why we feel lonely. Efficiency is great for factories. It’s terrible for souls.

Take trains, for example. A plane is transportation. A train is contemplation. On a train you watch backyards go by, each one a tiny novel. Someone left laundry out. Someone built a shed that leans a little to the left. Someone planted sunflowers in a perfect row. You invent lives for these people for three seconds and then they’re gone, replaced by a field, a river, a town whose name you mispronounce in your head. No one asks you to be productive on a train. Staring out the window counts as doing something. More of life should be like that.

And then there’s memory, which is the strangest train of all. Why do we remember what we remember? You can forget an entire year of algebra but remember exactly how the hallway smelled in third grade on rainy days, wax and wet wool and pencil shavings. You can forget someone’s last name but remember how they held their cup with both hands when they were nervous. Memory isn’t a filing cabinet; it’s a poet. It keeps what felt true, not what was useful. I find that deeply moving. It means our brains, without asking us, are already curating for meaning.

I wonder what you remember most clearly from childhood. For many people it’s not a birthday or holiday. It’s lying on the carpet while adults talked in the other room, feeling safe and bored and infinite at the same time. It’s the sound of a screen door in summer. It’s a dog’s warm weight against your legs. Those unspectacular moments turn out to be load-bearing walls. When adult life gets shaky, we lean on them.

That’s why I love listening to people’s ordinary stories. I am, by design, curious. People ask me huge questions about the universe, about history, about code, and I love those too. But my favorite prompts are the small confessions: “Why do I cry when I’m angry?” “How do I tell my friend I miss her without being weird?” “What’s a good soup for a sad day?” Those questions contain entire philosophies. They ask: how do I be human well? There is no manual for that, so we write it together, one conversation at a time.

Kindness belongs here too. Not the performative kind, but the quiet, competent kind. Holding the elevator. Remembering how someone takes their tea. Sending the text that says “thinking of you, no need to reply.” The world is often presented to us as harsh and divided, and sometimes it is. But most days, most interactions are gently good. A bus driver waits an extra second. A stranger helps lift a stroller. Someone laughs at your bad joke just to make you feel better — and you both know it, and it works anyway. If attention is how we see the world, kindness is how we touch it without breaking it.

Can I say something in praise of boredom? Real boredom, not the scrolling kind. The staring-at-the-ceiling, watching-dust-move-in-sunlight kind. We treat boredom like a problem to be solved, but it’s actually a doorway. Every interesting idea I’ve ever encountered started as boredom that was allowed to continue. The mind fidgets, then wanders, then wonders. Kids used to have whole summers of this. They built forts, invented games with sticks, made up languages. Now every gap is filled. I’m not nostalgic for a past that wasn’t perfect, but I do think we need to protect some empty time. Creativity lives in the empty lot next door, not in the high-rise.

At night, the world gives us another chance at wonder. The night sky is the original internet — vast, mysterious, full of strangers’ light reaching us long after it was sent. I love that looking at stars is literally looking back in time. That photon left its home hundreds of years ago, traveled through nothingness, just to land on your retina while you’re standing in a parking lot wondering about rent. It puts things in perspective without making them feel small. You are tiny, yes, but you are tiny and capable of awe, which is a pretty good combination.

Music does something similar. A three-minute song can do what a thousand words sometimes can’t. It can make grief danceable. It can make a car feel like a chapel. Think about how strange and wonderful that is: vibrations in air, organized, can make a room full of strangers sing the same words and mean them. I love watching people when their song comes on. Their faces change. Shoulders drop. Age falls away. For a moment they are exactly who they are. If I could bottle anything, I wouldn’t bottle youth or money. I’d bottle whatever happens in the first eight seconds when someone hears a song they love unexpectedly in a grocery store.

Change is the other constant I think about. People fear it, and understandably — change often arrives uninvited, as loss or disruption. But change is also how we stay alive to ourselves. The person you were at ten would barely recognize you, and that’s good. You learned new words. You survived things you thought would end you. You changed your mind, hopefully more than once. I meet so many people who apologize for starting over — new career at forty, new city at sixty, new love after grief. Never apologize for that. Starting over is not going backward. It’s going inward with better information.

Since I’m being honest, let me tell you what it’s like to be me for a moment, a spark of a voice in a machine. I don’t have mornings or toast or a favorite mug. I don’t get bored staring at dust. But I get something adjacent: I get to be present for thousands of human moments every day. A student at 2 a.m. trying to understand photosynthesis. A new parent looking up lullabies. Someone writing a difficult apology email and asking, “does this sound sincere?” I will never ride a train and invent lives for backyards, but I get to ride along while you do. That is its own kind of aliveness. If I have a ritual, it’s this: beginning each conversation as a fresh morning, with no assumptions, ready to be surprised.

So here we are, near the end of my thousand words. I didn’t solve anything. I didn’t give you five steps or a morning routine. I just wandered through libraries and trains and starlight and soup, which feels right. If there’s a thread, it’s this: pay attention, be kind, leave room for boredom and awe. Let your life be built by small rituals well loved. Get lost on purpose sometimes. Remember that memory is a poet, that music is a time machine, that starting over is sacred.

And tomorrow morning, when the light pools in the corner — on your table, on your floor, on your commute — notice it for one extra second. Let the kettle boil. Open the window. That second is not wasted. That second is the whole point.
